titel: Imago primi saeculi — the centenary emblem book (the title and one emblem from each book)
quelle: Antwerp: ex officina Plantiniana Balthasaris Moreti, 1640; images rendered from the Internet Archive scan imagoprimisaecul00boll (public domain), plates cropped from the page images. Latin transcribed by eye from the same pages (long s and the ae ligature normalised, u/v as printed); English: this site's unofficial working translations (CC0). The Dutch mirror pages come from the vernacular counterpart issued by the same press in the same year, the Af-Beeldinghe van d'eerste eeuwe der Societeyt Iesu, with Dutch verses by Adriaen Poirters SJ (Internet Archive afbeeldinghevand00boll, public domain); headings and rhymed glosses transcribed by eye.
hinweis: The iconographic path of the apparatus — unlike Calculemus, this corpus can carry images, and here it does: the engraved title and eleven emblems of the 1640 centenary volume — one from each of the six books, plus five deepenings — each with its lemma, its epigram distich by distich, and a working translation, and each closed by its Dutch mirror: the same plate in the Af-Beeldinghe of the same year, with Poirters's rhymed vernacular gloss. The Latin volume holds over 120 emblems in all; this selection is a spine, not a survey, and each emblem was chosen for what it touches elsewhere in the corpus. Part of the concordance and the citation-bound dialogue; not part of the linguistic statistics, which describe the core corpus only.

sections.blurb: The Society enthroned under the IHS, with the six books of her first century in medallions around her.

units.alt: Engraved title of the Imago primi saeculi (Antwerp 1640): the Society personified, crowned with the IHS monogram, above the Plantin imprint of Balthasar Moretus; putti carry the medallions of the six books and banderoles of the Doctors, Martyrs and Virgins.
units.en: The engraved title, by the Galle workshop for the Plantin press: the Society sits enthroned as a crowned figure bearing the IHS, her titulus reading 'Imago primi saeculi Societatis Iesu a Provincia Flandro-Belgica eiusdem Societatis repraesentata' — the image of the Society's first century, presented by its Flemish-Belgian province. Around her, putti display six emblem medallions, one for each book of the volume: the Society born, growing, working, suffering, honoured, and the province itself. The imprint reads 'Antverpiae ex officina Plantiniana Balthasaris Moreti, anno Societatis saeculari M.DC.XL' — in the Society's centenary year, 1640. Everything the volume's critics would later mock is already here: the scale, the self-confidence, the apparatus of triumph.
units.label: The engraved title of 1640

sections.titel: Book I · Nouum mutor in alitem — The renewal of the spirit (p. 200)
sections.blurb: The silkworm emblem, from Societas nascens: Horace’s metamorphosis turned to the renovation of vows — enclosure not as prison but as the workshop of wings.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 200: in a cartouche, a butterfly breaks out of the silkworm’s cocoon in an open landscape.
units.orig: Renouatio spiritus. — Nouum mutor in alitem. Horat.
units.en: The renewal of the spirit. — I am changed into a new winged creature. The lemma adapts Horace (Odes II 20, 'album mutor in alitem'); the engraving gives the ode's swan to the silkworm, and the renewal to the yearly renovation of vows and spirit in the Society's houses.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Vix bene conclusit proprio se carcere bombyx, / Et nouus inde tibi protinus ales adest.
units.en: Scarcely has the silkworm shut itself into the prison of its own making, when out of it, all at once, a new winged creature stands before you.

units.orig: Iam vigor, & volucres creuere in tergora pennae: / Qui modo serpebat, si lubet, ecce volat.
units.en: Now there is strength, and flying feathers have grown upon its back: what just now crept — look, if it pleases — flies.

units.orig: Nempe sibi talem format natura recessum, / Remigij alarum quo fabricetur opus.
units.en: For nature shapes itself such a retreat precisely so that the oarage of wings may be built within it.

units.orig: Ite agite, & sacris, Socij, vos claudite septis, / Roboris aetherei crescat vt inde vigor.
units.en: Go then, companions, and shut yourselves within the sacred enclosures, that from there the strength of heavenly vigour may grow.

units.orig: Innouat hîc vires, hîc sacrae semina flammae / Sufficit, hîc alas Daedalus aptat amor.
units.en: Here love renews strength, here it supplies the seeds of the sacred flame, here — a Daedalus — it fits on the wings.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 136: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 136
units.orig: Vernieuwinghe vanden gheest. — Te voren kroop, / Nu vliegh en loop.
units.en: Renewal of the spirit. — 'Before, I crept; now I fly and run.'

sections.titel: Book I · Nexus non sufficit vnus — One bond is not enough (p. 199)
sections.blurb: The ivy on the oak, the silkworm’s neighbour on the facing page: the renewal of vows as love multiplying its own chains — and the third of the volume’s “non sufficit” lemmata carried here.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 199: ivy winds up an oak in an open landscape, its tendrils circling trunk and branches.
units.orig: Renouatio votorum. — Nexus non sufficit vnus.
units.en: The renewal of vows. — One bond is not enough. The third of the volume's 'non sufficit' lemmata carried here: one world (E1), one fire (E5) — and one bond. The ivy on the oak as the yearly renewal of the vows: love multiplies its own chains.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Nulla quies in amore datur: quis comprimat ignem? / Feruida flamma moras, otia nescit amor.
units.en: No rest is granted in love — who could smother its fire? A glowing flame knows no delays; love knows no idleness.

units.orig: Siqua potest cessasse, potest periisse fauilla; / Deses ab extincto proximus ardor erit.
units.en: A spark that can pause can also have died; an idle burning is next neighbour to one put out.

units.orig: Pectus amans, triplici quamuis adamante reuinxit, / Haec mage, dum renouat vincula, stringit amor.
units.en: Though love has bound the loving breast with triple adamant, it draws those chains the tighter each time it renews them.

units.orig: Vultus alit, flammasque nouas, noua spicula vibrat, / Amplexuque nouo vincula multiplicat.
units.en: It feeds its gaze, brandishes new flames and new darts, and with every new embrace multiplies the bonds.

units.orig: Et quoties sacros, sua vota, retractat amores, / Et quoties renouat gaudia, vincla facit.
units.en: And as often as it takes up again its sacred loves — its vows — as often as it renews its joys, it forges chains.

units.orig: Sic hederae, iuncta quamuis radice ligantur, / Et trunco teneras applicuere comas;
units.en: So the ivies: though they are tied to it by a joined root, and have laid their tender tresses on the trunk,

units.orig: Assurgunt, ramosque nouis complexibus vrgent, / Quaque patet quercus, Bacchica serta gerit:
units.en: they climb, press the branches with new embraces, and wherever the oak spreads it wears the garlands of Bacchus:

units.orig: Non hederae, nexus non sufficit vnus amori: / Mille hederae amplexus, mille requirit amor.
units.en: For the ivy — for love — one bond is not enough: the ivy asks a thousand embraces, and love a thousand.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 134: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 134
units.orig: Vernieuwinghe der beloften. — Het maeckt hem vast, / Soo langh het wast.
units.en: Renewal of the vows. — 'It binds him fast, as long as it grows.'

sections.titel: Book II · Vnus non sufficit orbis — One world is not enough (p. 326)
sections.blurb: The emblem of the Indian missions, from Societas crescens: the boy with two globes, against Alexander who halted at the Ganges. The most quoted — and most mocked — line of the whole volume.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 326: a winged genius stands between two globes — the old world and the new — holding a bow, his arrow pointing across them.
units.orig: Societatis Missiones Indicae. — Vnus non sufficit orbis.
units.en: The missions of the Society to the Indies. — One world is not enough. The lemma adapts Juvenal on Alexander (Sat. X 168: 'unus Pellaeo iuveni non sufficit orbis'); the epigram makes the comparison explicit.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Esse quid hoc dicam generosae mentis? vtrumque / Hic puer amplexus expedit ante globum.
units.en: What shall I call this but greatness of mind? This boy holds both globes clasped before him.

units.orig: Dic puer, an toto pectus tibi latius orbe est, / Et minor est animo mundus vterque tuo?
units.en: Say, boy — is your breast wider than the whole world, and are both worlds together smaller than your spirit?

units.orig: Sic quondam AEmathio iuueni par non fuit orbis; / Et quo non potuit praelia, vota tulit.
units.en: So once the world was no match for the Emathian youth: where he could not carry war, he carried wishes.

units.orig: Ille tamen victor Regnorum, ad flumina Gangis / Constitit, & magno victus ab orbe fuit.
units.en: Yet he, the conqueror of kingdoms, halted at the streams of the Ganges, and by the greatness of the world was himself conquered.

units.orig: Maior amor Gangem superans, pelagusque profundum, / Victor in extremis finibus orbis agit.
units.en: A greater love overcomes the Ganges and the deep sea, and works as conqueror at the farthest ends of the earth.

units.orig: Illius in castris qui signa sequuntur IESV / (Ignauus tali quis velit esse duce?)
units.en: Those who follow the standards of JESUS in his camp — who would consent to be idle under such a leader? —

units.orig: Quid mirum, Herculeas vltra ac freta vasta columnas, / Quaerere & Eoos, quaerere & Hesperios?
units.en: what wonder that, beyond the columns of Hercules and the vast straits, they seek out the peoples of the dawn and of the evening alike?

units.orig: Dius amor nullis arctatur finibus; illos / Igneus Ignatî spiritus intus agit.
units.en: Divine love is straitened by no boundaries: the fiery spirit of Ignatius drives them on from within.

units.orig: Exemplum ducis, atque animarum lucra decusque, / Et magno in terris fixa trophaea Deo,
units.en: Their leader's example, the winning of souls and its honour, and trophies planted on earth to the great God,

units.orig: Ingentes animos faciunt, quos expleat vnus / Qui dulci recreat numine corda Deus.
units.en: make their spirits vast — spirits that only the one God can fill, who refreshes hearts with his sweet presence.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 204: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 204
units.orig: De Seyndinghe nae Indien. — Een alleen / VVas my te kleen.
units.en: The mission to the Indies. — 'One alone was too small for me.'

sections.titel: Book II · Nec segnior altera cura est Antipodum — The setting sun (p. 327)
sections.blurb: The facing page of E1: the sun goes down between the columns of Hercules — not dying, but crossing to light the Antipodes. The missions to the New World as the second half of the day.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 327: the sun sets into the sea between the two columns of Hercules, its rays still filling the sky over an empty shore.
units.orig: Missiones noui Orbis. — Nec segnior altera cura est Antipodum.
units.en: The missions of the New World. — Nor is the other care, for the Antipodes, any slower. The facing page of E1: the setting sun does not die but goes to light the other hemisphere — Hercules' columns, the old edge of the world, stand open.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Aurea ab Eois Phoebi lux fulserat vndis, / Grataque lux oculis fulserat ista meis:
units.en: Golden had Phoebus's light flashed up from the eastern waves, and welcome had that light flashed upon my eyes:

units.orig: Reddiderat mundoque diem, rebusque colorem, / Ridebat toto multus in orbe nitor:
units.en: it had given the world back its day and things their colour, and a full radiance laughed over the whole earth.

units.orig: Tunc ego: Sic semper rutiles, pulcherrime Titan, / Neu caput auricomum condere nocte velis.
units.en: Then said I: So may you glow for ever, fairest Titan — and never wish to bury your golden-haired head in night.

units.orig: Quae, precor, inuidia est radios subducere terris, / Ac tenebris toties praecipitare diem?
units.en: What envy is it, I pray, to withdraw your rays from the lands, and so often to hurl the day down into darkness?

units.orig: Nil ago: iam praeceps deuexo fertur Olympo, / Et iam caeruleo Phoebus in amne latet:
units.en: I plead in vain: already Phoebus is carried headlong down the sloping sky, and already he hides in the dark-blue stream;

units.orig: Mox etiam furuo texerunt nubila caelum / Syrmate, & in toto nox fuit vna polo.
units.en: soon the clouds covered the sky with their dusky train, and one single night lay over the whole pole.

units.orig: Vt vidi infrendens, Sol o pulcherrime, dixi, / Exsere nube caput: quae tibi caussa fugae est?
units.en: When I saw it, gnashing my teeth I said: O fairest Sun, put your head out of the cloud — what reason have you for flight?

units.orig: Forsitan Hesperium fessus (quae fabula vatum est) / Luminis vt repares damna, cubile petis?
units.en: Perhaps, weary, you seek your western couch (so runs the poets’ fable), to repair the losses of your light?

units.orig: Fallimur: Antipodum non segnior altera cura est, / Nec tantum nostro diuidis orbe diem.
units.en: We are deceived: your other care, for the Antipodes, is no slower — you do not deal out the day to our world alone.

units.orig: Et miramur adhuc te, Loiolaea propago, / Tendere in oppositae dissita Regna plagae?
units.en: And do we still wonder, offspring of Loyola, that you stretch toward the far-scattered kingdoms of the opposite quarter?

units.orig: Scilicet hoc quoque solis habes, nec segnior illo es; / Hinc alia ex alia te quoque cura vocat.
units.en: This too, of course, you have of the sun — nor are you slower than he: from here one care after another calls you also on.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 206: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 206
units.orig: De Seyndinghe nae de Nieuwe wereldt. — De minne-straelen / En vinden gheen paelen.
units.en: The mission to the New World. — 'The rays of love find no boundary posts.'

sections.titel: Book III · Omnibus omnia — All things to all (p. 452)
sections.blurb: The mirror emblem, from Societas agens: 1 Corinthians 9:22 as the workers’ motto — adaptation without flattery, likeness without deceit. Ignatius’s rules of dealing (Letter XII), drawn.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 452: a mirror stands in a tiled room between two herm figures, reflecting the light of a window.
units.orig: Societatis operarij. — Omnibus omnia.
units.en: The workers of the Society. — All things to all (1 Corinthians 9:22). The mirror as the Jesuit worker: it takes on every likeness without flattery and without deceit — the epigram is a small treatise on the adaptability Ignatius taught in the instruction for Ireland (Letter XII) and Xavier practised from Comorin to Japan.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Qualiter in speculo facies, motusque relucent, / Aduersasque refert laeuis imago notas;
units.en: As a face and its motions shine back in a mirror, and the smooth image returns your marks reversed,

units.orig: Haud aliter formas hominum se vertit in omnes, / Omnibus vt solers omnia fiat amor:
units.en: just so does love turn itself into all the shapes of men, that, all-skilled, it may become all things to all:

units.orig: Castus amor, castis quem mentibus indit IESVS, / Ignati sacro quae prius igne calent:
units.en: chaste love, which JESUS plants in chaste minds — minds already glowing with Ignatius's sacred fire.

units.orig: Omnia diuersae capit hic simulacra figurae, / Omnia compositis reddit imaginibus.
units.en: It takes in every likeness of every different figure, and gives them all back in answering images.

units.orig: Nec tamen in similes trahit assentatio mores: / Nec studet occultis ille nocere dolis.
units.en: And yet it is no flattery that draws it into like manners, nor does it seek to harm by hidden wiles.

units.orig: Fallere nescit amor, numquam sibi dissidet ipse, / Ingenio similis sit licet vsque tuo.
units.en: Love cannot deceive; it is never at odds with itself, though it grow ever so like your own temper.

units.orig: Assumet tecum, tecum sua gaudia ponet, / Cum puero ludet, cum sene tristis erit.
units.en: It will take up your ways with you, and with you lay its joys aside; with the boy it will play, with the old man it will be grave.

units.orig: Institor extremis merces accersis ab Indis? / Impiger ignoto littore quaeret opes.
units.en: Are you a trader fetching wares from farthest India? Untiring, it will seek out goods on the unknown shore beside you.

units.orig: Si victor redeas, laetos canet ille triumphos: / Tecum per terras, per mare, bella geret.
units.en: If you come home a victor, it will sing your glad triumphs; with you it will wage wars by land and by sea.

units.orig: Desertas etiam siluas montesque pererrat / Fidus amor, tamquam barbarus ingenio.
units.en: Faithful love wanders even deserted woods and mountains, as though itself barbarous in temper.

units.orig: Nempe vt possit amor similes sibi reddere cunctos, / Dissimilis toties redditur ipse sibi.
units.en: For this — that love may render all men like itself — it is rendered, just as many times, unlike itself.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 258: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 258
units.orig: Werck-lieden der Societeyt. — Ghelijck / Aen ieghelijck.
units.en: The workmen of the Society. — 'Like unto everyone.'

sections.titel: Book III · Hac monstrat eundum — The book that shows the way (p. 459)
sections.blurb: From Societas agens: the little book of the Exercises as the surest guide for the choice of a state of life — a wayside Mercury for the election, surer than Ariadne’s thread or the Pharos.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 459: a traveller at a parting of ways looks up to a statue of Mercury on a pedestal, its arm pointing out the road; crosses mark the false paths.
units.orig: Libellus Exercitiorum dux certissimus ad eligendum vitae statum. — Hac monstrat eundum.
units.en: The little book of the Exercises, the surest guide for choosing a state of life. — This way, it shows, one must go. A wayside Mercury for the book of the election: the apparatus's own core text, drawn as an emblem by the Society's centenary.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: In varias dissecta vias se semita pandit, / Et longis circum flexibus errat iter:
units.en: The footpath splits and spreads into many ways, and the road wanders all about in long windings:

units.orig: Cumque tibi dubius centum diuortia trames / Praebeat, e centum est vna tenenda via.
units.en: and though the doubtful track offer you a hundred partings, of the hundred there is one way to be held.

units.orig: Si semel incerto per deuia calle feraris, / Certa tuum cingent mille pericla caput.
units.en: If once you are carried down an uncertain path into trackless country, a thousand certain dangers will ring your head.

units.orig: Haec vrsis insessa, feros tegit illa leones, / Hic fallit caecos subdola fossa pedes.
units.en: This road is beset with bears, that one hides savage lions; here a treacherous ditch cheats unseeing feet.

units.orig: Ad caput illa redit crebro perplexa recursu, / Ista viatorum silua cruore madet.
units.en: That one, tangled, runs back again and again to its own beginning; that wood is soaked with the blood of travellers.

units.orig: O! quis in hoc ductor discrimine fila ministret, / Aut Ariadnaeo stamine signet iter?
units.en: Oh, what guide in this peril will hand us the threads, or mark out the way with Ariadne's clew?

units.orig: Nocte Pharos inter Mareotica saxa regebat / Lumine deprensas officiosa rates.
units.en: By night the Pharos, dutiful with its light, steered among the Mareotic rocks the ships it caught sight of;

units.orig: Isacidas fluctus inter ducebat Erythrae / Designans facilem praeuia flamma fugam.
units.en: among the waves of the Red Sea a flame going before led the sons of Israel, tracing out an easy flight.

units.orig: Parce queri: tibi iam positis Ignatius armis / Caelesti rutilam praetulit igne facem.
units.en: Cease complaining: Ignatius, his weapons now laid down, has carried before you a torch glowing with heavenly fire.

units.orig: Paruus mole liber, sed rerum pondere magnus, / Non dubia cupidum ducet ad astra via.
units.en: A book small in bulk but great in the weight of its matter will lead the longing soul to the stars by no uncertain way.

units.orig: Ne violis, ne crede rosis: hac monstrat eundum, / Saeuit vbi in teneros plurima spina pedes.
units.en: Trust neither the violets nor the roses: this way, it shows, one must go — where many a thorn rages against tender feet.

units.orig: Hoc duce nec Pharios ignes, nec fila requires: / Certior hic Cresso stamine ductor erit.
units.en: With this guide you will need neither the fires of Pharos nor the threads: this guide will be surer than the Cretan clew.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 270: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 270
units.orig: Het boecksken vande gheestelijcke Oeffeninghen is eenen sekeren leydts-man om eenen staet des leuens te verkiesen. — Vraeght hier raedt, / Eer ghy gaet.
units.en: The little book of the Spiritual Exercises is a sure guide for choosing a state of life. — 'Ask counsel here, before you go.'

sections.titel: Book IV · Solem nulla sagitta ferit — No arrow strikes the sun (p. 565)
sections.blurb: From Societas patiens: fools shooting arrows at the sun — the Society’s answer to its attackers, printed while the Monita secreta and the pamphlets circulated. The counter-voices, seen from inside.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 565: four fools in motley shoot arrows at the sun; the arrows turn in the air and fall back toward the archers.
units.orig: Societas frustra oppugnatur ab inuidis. — Solem nulla sagitta ferit.
units.en: The Society is attacked by the envious in vain. — No arrow strikes the sun. The Society's own answer, in 1640, to a century of Monita, pamphlets and polemic: read it beside the counter-voices this apparatus carries — and note that the archers are drawn as fools.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Stulte, quid in caelum non peruenientia mittis / Tela? quid insano praelia Marte geris?
units.en: Fool, why do you shoot at the sky weapons that will never arrive? Why wage battles under a madman's Mars?

units.orig: Laedere ne solem possis, locus ipse tuetur; / Immensa nostro distat ab orbe via.
units.en: Its very place protects the sun from your wounding: it stands an immeasurable way from our world.

units.orig: Caucasus excelso licet imponatur Olympo, / Et super hos vastus Pelion Ossa premat:
units.en: Though Caucasus be piled on high Olympus, and above them vast Pelion press down upon Ossa,

units.orig: Non secus ac ima positus si valle maneres, / In stolidum recident spicula missa caput.
units.en: no differently than if you stood in the deepest valley, the darts you send will fall back on your stupid head.

units.orig: Tangere fac possis, radiorum luce corusca / Hostem ne videas impediere tuum.
units.en: Suppose you could reach it: the flashing light of its rays will keep you from so much as seeing your enemy.

units.orig: Fallere, si solem spectare haec carmina credis: / Stultitiam damnant, liuida turba, tuam.
units.en: You deceive yourself if you think these verses concern the sun: it is your folly they condemn, you envious crowd.

units.orig: Liuor iners claris Heroum detrahit ausis, / Et iaculo solem non feriente petit.
units.en: Sluggish envy disparages the shining deeds of heroes, and aims at the sun with a javelin that never strikes.

units.orig: Si coeant, quotquot tam dira insania versat, / Non legio in terris grandior vlla foret.
units.en: If all whom so dire a madness drives were to band together, no legion on earth would be greater.

units.orig: Sed tamen inuictae IESV sub nomine turmae / Hoc genus ante alios vimque manusque parat.
units.en: And yet it is against the unconquered squadrons under the name of JESUS that this breed, before all others, readies its force and its hands.

units.orig: Quisquis es, insanis frustra conatibus vti / Desine: nam Solem nulla sagitta ferit.
units.en: Whoever you are, cease to spend mad efforts in vain: for no arrow strikes the sun.

units.orig: Despicit ex alta vesanos arce furores; / Et ferit auctores missa sagitta suos.
units.en: From its high citadel it looks down on the ravings of the frenzied; and the arrow that was shot strikes those who sent it.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 388: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 388
units.orig: De Societeyt wordt te vergheefs vande benijders bevochten. — Als 't Gode behaeght, / Beter benijdt, dan beklaeght.
units.en: The Society is assailed by the envious in vain. — 'As it pleases God: better envied than pitied.'

sections.titel: Book IV · Dant vincla decorem — Bonds give beauty (p. 577)
sections.blurb: The tied carnation: prisons and chains as the Society’s ornament. The deliberate friction of the corpus — read it beside the Cautio Criminalis of 1631, where a Jesuit counts what chains actually did.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 577: carnations in a pot, bound upright to sticks — the tied flower blooming the fairer for its bonds.
units.orig: Societatem carceres & vincula cohonestant. — Dant vincla decorem.
units.en: Prisons and chains do the Society honour. — Bonds give beauty. The pictura is a flower-pot: carnations tied to their sticks bloom the fairer. Read this beside the Cautio Criminalis, printed nine years earlier by a member of the same order: what the emblem wears as ornament, Dubium LI counts link by link.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Turpe catenati, si certa est culpa, nocentes; / Vincula dedecorant, quae meruere, manus.
units.en: Shameful are the chained when the guilt is certain; chains disgrace the hands that have deserved them.

units.orig: Infamis tetro procedit carcere, cuius / Ante fuit foedo crimine laesus honor.
units.en: He walks infamous out of the foul prison whose honour was wounded beforehand by a foul crime.

units.orig: Quam bene felici stringuntur brachia neruo, / Libera quae summi Iudicis vrna probat?
units.en: But how well are those arms bound with a happy cord which the urn of the highest Judge pronounces free?

units.orig: Vincula virtutem, virtutem carcer honorat; / Scilicet inde noui lucra decoris habet.
units.en: Chains honour virtue, and prison honours it: from there, indeed, it draws the gain of a new beauty.

units.orig: Vt flos, cui grati similis consensus odoris / Caryophyllorum nomen habere dedit:
units.en: Like the flower to which the like agreement of its pleasing scent has given the name of the carnation:

units.orig: Ille, licet nitida variat tot fronde colores, / Primus honor Florae deliciumque suae;
units.en: though it varies so many colours on its shining leafage, first honour of Flora and her darling,

units.orig: Et forma tantum flores supereminet omnes, / Quantum vel Paphias vincit odore rosas;
units.en: and in beauty overtops all flowers by as much as it outdoes even the Paphian roses in scent —

units.orig: Si tamen obseptum vinclis & crate coerces, / Nescio quid paruo a carcere maius habet.
units.en: yet if you hedge it in and hold it fast with bonds and trellis, it takes from its little prison a something greater still.

units.orig: Tu quoque progenies Loiola digna parente, / Clarior a vinclis compedibusque redis.
units.en: You too, offspring worthy of Loyola your parent, come back the brighter from chains and fetters.

units.orig: Emicat in flammas specubus calor abditus atris: / Pulchrius obscura sidera nocte micant.
units.en: Heat hidden in black caverns leaps out into flame; the stars glitter more beautifully in the dark of night.

units.orig: Te quoque condecorant habitata nocentibus antra; / Nec minus his virtus clausa nitoris habet.
units.en: You too are adorned by dungeons that the guilty have inhabited; and virtue shut inside them has no less of splendour.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 408: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 408
units.orig: De boeyen en banden strecken de Societeyt tot eere. — Gheen banden / Van schanden.
units.en: Fetters and bonds serve the Society for honour. — 'No bonds of shame.'

sections.titel: Book V · Solus non sufficit ignis — The forging of Xavier (p. 717)
sections.blurb: From Societas honorata: Ignatius as smith, Xavier as the iron, and Peter Favre — faber, the smith’s own name — as the added hand. Three works of this corpus in one engraving.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 717: a smith at his forge works a glowing piece of iron on the anvil, the furnace blazing behind him.
units.orig: Ignatius P. Fabrum adhibet ad conuersionem Xauerij. — Solus non sufficit ignis.
units.en: Ignatius employs Father Faber for the conversion of Xavier. — Fire alone does not suffice. The lemma answers the volume's own most famous line ('one world is not enough'), and the whole epigram turns on a double sense the engraving keeps visible: faber is the smith at the anvil, and Faber is Peter Favre — whose journal this apparatus carries — the added hand by which Ignatius's fire finally forged Xavier.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Arte opus Ignati: solus non sufficit ignis: / Arte opus est: flectes arte, quod igne nequis.
units.en: Art is needed, Ignatius — fire alone does not suffice. Art is needed: by art you will bend what you cannot bend by fire.

units.orig: Vidi ego, caelatum clypei cum fingeret orbem, / Non solo ferrum molliit igne faber.
units.en: I once watched a smith shaping the embossed circle of a shield: he softened the iron not by fire alone.

units.orig: Non labor vnus erat: pars vrget follibus auras, / Mersaque stridenti temperat aera lacu;
units.en: It was not one labour: one hand drives the air with the bellows and tempers the plunged bronze in the hissing trough;

units.orig: Pars massam exercet, pars altera forcipe versat, / Haec duris aptat cotibus, illa terit.
units.en: one works the mass, another turns it with the tongs; this one sets it to the hard whetstones, that one grinds.

units.orig: Manabat plenis sudor per corpora riuis: / Vsque adeo multa flectitur arte chalybs.
units.en: Sweat ran down their bodies in full streams: so much art it takes to bend steel.

units.orig: Aestuat, & valido flagrat Xauerius igne; / Formari solo non tamen igne valet.
units.en: Xavier seethes and blazes with a strong fire; yet by fire alone he cannot be formed.

units.orig: Verum vbi solertis Fabri manus addita, sese / In partem duci quamlibet arte sinit.
units.en: But once the hand of the skilful smith — of Faber — is added, he lets himself be guided by art into any shape whatever.

units.orig: Adspice vt immissos exercet spiritus ignes, / Totaque flammato massa recocta foco est.
units.en: See how the blast plies the fires let into him, and the whole mass is forged anew in the flaming hearth.

units.orig: Ardentes animos (animus stridoribus ardens / Proditur) iniectae temperat imber aquae.
units.en: A shower of water, thrown on, tempers the burning spirit — for a spirit on fire betrays itself by its hissing.

units.orig: Quem gemitum referunt auditi incudibus ictus? / Qua non exhaustus sedulitate labor?
units.en: What a groan the blows give back, heard upon the anvils! What diligence has this labour not spent?

units.orig: Mille operum Faber est: nec respirare potestas. / Tantae Xauerium fingere molis erat.
units.en: The Smith is a smith of a thousand tasks, with no leave to draw breath: so great a work was it to fashion Xavier.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 508: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 508
units.orig: Ignatius ghebruyckt Faber, alias Smidt, tot de bekeeringhe van Xauerius. — Al is 't vier vverm, / 't Vereyscht 's smits erm.
units.en: Ignatius employs Faber — alias Smith — for the conversion of Xavier. — 'Though the fire be warm, it needs the smith's arm.' The Dutch page spells the pun out in its heading.

units.orig: Den hamer en het vier, die moeten samen wercken, / En met eenpaerigh hulp malckanderen verstercken: / 't Een maeckt het ijser heet, en 't ander gheeft den slagh, / Soo krijght het een nieuw vorm dat inden oven lagh. / VVant schoon den gauwen knecht den blaesbalgh treckt met lusten, / En dat den meester self de kolen niet laet rusten, / Maer meer en meer onsteeckt den ouergrooten brandt, / Komt daer gheen slagh omtrent, het ijser houdt sijn standt.
units.en: Poirters's first stanza, translated: 'The hammer and the fire must work together, and with united help strengthen one another: the one makes the iron hot, the other gives the blow — so what lay in the furnace receives a new form. For though the quick apprentice pulls the bellows with a will, and the master himself lets the coals take no rest but kindles the great blaze more and more: if no blow comes near it, the iron keeps its old shape.' The stanza continues on the next page of the print.
units.label: Poirters's Dutch verse, first stanza (p. 508)

sections.titel: Book V · Tum te terra teget — The death of Xavier as an eclipse (p. 721)
sections.blurb: The answer to E1, four hundred pages on: the boy who held two globes dies at the gate of China, and the epigram reads his death as the eclipse of a full moon. Beside it belongs the last letter, FX IV.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 721: an eclipse darkens the sky over the sea — a dark shrouded form against the stars, the moon below on the water.
units.orig: Xauerius, orbe peragrato, moritur in littore Chinarum. — Tum te terra teget, cum totum impleueris orbem.
units.en: Xavier, having traversed the world, dies on the shore of China. — Then only shall earth cover you, when you have filled the whole world. The emblem answers E1: the boy who held two globes ends at Sancian, and the epigram reads his death as an eclipse — read it beside the last letter, FX IV.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Cingite fronde caput: Xauerius orbe laboris / Deficit impleto: cingite fronde caput.
units.en: Wreathe his head with leaves: Xavier fails only when the circuit of his labour is filled — wreathe his head with leaves.

units.orig: Amplius ille nihil potuit superaddere coeptis: / Tota peragrata est India, iam satis est.
units.en: He could add nothing more to what he had begun: the whole of India is traversed; now it is enough.

units.orig: Chinae, Goa, Iapon, Ternata, Moluca, tot vrbes, / Quae toties initae caussa fuere viae;
units.en: China, Goa, Japan, Ternate, the Moluccas — so many cities that were, so many times, the reason for setting out;

units.orig: Totque aliae gentes, tot primo subdita Phoebo / Littora, sudoris plus habuere satis.
units.en: and so many other peoples, so many shores that lie under the morning sun, have had more than their fill of his sweat.

units.orig: Ergo vel extremam cum nil superesset ad Eon; / Ipsis terrarum finibus immoritur.
units.en: And so, when nothing remained short of the uttermost East, he dies upon the very ends of the earth.

units.orig: Immoritur votis ingentibus, orbe repleto: / Cynthia sic etiam plena perire solet.
units.en: He dies upon his vast desires, the world now filled: so even Cynthia — the moon — is wont to perish at her fullest.

units.orig: Cynthia terrarum, caeli Franciscus ab vmbra / Palluit: exanimis vultus, amantis erat.
units.en: The moon grows pale in the shadow of the earth; Francis paled in the shadow of heaven — and the lifeless face was a lover's face.

units.orig: Obruitur tenebris & furua Cynthia nube: / Franciscus radiis obruit astra suis.
units.en: Cynthia is buried in darkness and a dusky cloud: Francis buries the stars beneath rays of his own.

units.orig: Non iubar hoc magicae carmen tenuauerit artis: / Nil opus ad numeros aera repulsa sonent:
units.en: No spell of magic art shall thin this radiance; no need for the beaten bronze to clash out its rescuing rhythms:

units.orig: Perstat, & integros vbi vita reliquerit artus, / Maius ab extincto corpore lumen erit.
units.en: It stands fast; and when life has left the limbs — left them whole — the light from the extinguished body will be the greater.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 514: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 514
units.orig: Xauerius de wereldt doorreyst hebbende, sterft inden ingangh van China. — Als de ronde is ghedaen, / Sult ghy onder d'aerde gaen.
units.en: Xavier, having journeyed through the world, dies at the gate of China. — 'When the round is done, you shall go under the earth.'

sections.titel: Book VI · Da mihi animas, cetera tolle tibi — The army mission (p. 941)
sections.blurb: From the Flemish province’s own book: Abraham refusing the spoils of Sodom and keeping only the persons — Genesis 14:21 as the emblem of the camp chaplains.

units.alt: Emblem engraving, Imago primi saeculi p. 941: Abraham, returned from battle with his armed men, faces the crowned king of Sodom over a heap of captured vessels; the king gestures toward the freed captives.
units.orig: Missio Castrensis. — Da mihi animas, cetera tolle tibi.
units.en: The mission to the army camps. — Give me the souls, take the rest for yourself (Genesis 14:21). The Flemish province's emblem for its army chaplains: Abraham refusing the spoils of Sodom, keeping only the persons — a verse with a long afterlife as a motto of pastoral care.
units.label: The emblem and its lemma

units.orig: Hinc venit Assyria & Babylonis robur in armis; / Inde Gomorrhaei stant Sodomaeque duces.
units.en: From this side come Assyria and the strength of Babylon in arms; on that side stand the captains of Gomorrah and Sodom.

units.orig: Insonuere tubae: miscent certamina Reges: / Alterno late sanguine terra madet.
units.en: The trumpets have sounded; the kings join battle; far and wide the earth is soaked with the blood of both.

units.orig: Iam Sodomae cecidere Duces; iam vincula passi, / Felices socios qui cecidere vocant.
units.en: Now Sodom's captains have fallen; now those who suffer chains call happy the comrades who fell.

units.orig: Immeritum quoque Lot tristis fortuna coegit / Barbara captiua vincula ferre manu.
units.en: Undeserving Lot too a sad fortune has forced to bear barbarous chains upon his captive hands.

units.orig: Non tulit hanc sortem, neque tantum dedecus Abram: / Hoc duce tercentum, stant noua castra, viri.
units.en: Abram did not endure this lot, nor so great a disgrace: under his lead three hundred men stand up, a new camp.

units.orig: Vae tibi, vae Babylon, nostra quae clade superbis: / Iam rerum versas experiere vices.
units.en: Woe to you, woe, Babylon, who vaunt yourself upon our ruin: now you shall learn how fortunes turn.

units.orig: Assyrij cecidere; Loti iam vincula stringunt / Assyrios; Sodomae reddita praeda Duci est.
units.en: The Assyrians have fallen; Lot's chains now bind the Assyrians; the booty of Sodom is restored to its captain.

units.orig: Victor Abramus ouat: cui Rex: Age, diuide praedas, / Redde animas nobis, cetera tolle tibi.
units.en: Abram triumphs as victor; and to him the king: Come, divide the spoils — give the souls back to us, take the rest for yourself.

units.orig: Dicite vos Socij, vos Regia castra secuti, / Quae referet vester praemia digna labor?
units.en: Say, you Companions, you who have followed the King's camp: what worthy rewards shall your labour bring home?

units.orig: Quo lucro stabit victoria? dicite Regi: / Da nobis animas, cetera tolle tibi.
units.en: At what gain shall the victory stand? Say to the King: give us the souls, take the rest for yourself.

units.orig: Praemia non leuium ferimus satis ampla laborum, / Si nostra constet vita aliena salus.
units.en: We carry home rewards ample enough for no light labours, if another's salvation is bought at the price of our own life.

units.alt: The same emblem in the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe of 1640, p. 690: the plate re-engraved smaller, above the Latin lemma with a rhymed Dutch gloss and the vernacular verse of Adriaen Poirters.
units.label: The Dutch mirror — Af-Beeldinghe 1640, p. 690
units.orig: De Seyndinghe nae 't legher. — Der sielen buyt / Kies ick voor uyt.
units.en: The mission to the army. — 'The booty of souls I choose first.'
